steps.title: Apply Boyle's law
steps.narration: At constant temperature, pressure times volume stays constant.

steps.title: Substitute values
steps.narration: Put in P, V, and half of P for the new pressure.

steps.title: Solve for volume
steps.narration: Cancel P on both sides and multiply by two to get two V.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the starting pressure P, starting volume V, and the new pressure, which is half of P. Temperature and gas amount do not change.

teach.title: State Boyle's law
teach.narration: Use Boyle's law because temperature and moles are fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions.

teach.title: Substitute into equation
teach.narration: Replace the initial values with P and V, and replace the final pressure with P over two so we can find the new volume.

teach.title: Solve for new volume
teach.narration: Divide both sides by P over two. The P cancels out, and dividing by half doubles the volume to two V.

steps.title: Write configuration
steps.narration: Nitrogen has seven electrons arranged as one s two, two s two, two p three.

steps.title: Fill 2p orbitals
steps.narration: By Hund's rule, the three 2p electrons enter three separate orbitals singly.

steps.title: Count unpaired electrons
steps.narration: All three 2p electrons remain unpaired, giving three unpaired electrons.

teach.title: Find electron count
teach.narration: A neutral nitrogen atom has atomic number seven, which means it holds seven electrons in total.

teach.title: Fill energy levels
teach.narration: Place electrons into the lowest energy subshells first. Two fill the 1s orbital, two fill the 2s orbital, and three remain in the 2p subshell.

teach.title: Check paired inner shells
teach.narration: Both the 1s and 2s orbitals are completely full, so their electrons are already paired up and contribute zero unpaired electrons.

teach.title: Apply Hund's rule
teach.narration: The 2p subshell has three orbitals of equal energy. By Hund's rule, electrons spread into separate orbitals with parallel spins before any pairing occurs.

teach.title: Count unpaired electrons
teach.narration: Each of the three 2p orbitals holds one single electron, so a ground-state nitrogen atom has three unpaired electrons.

steps.title: Read atomic number
steps.narration: The atomic number of the isotope is fifteen.

steps.title: Relate Z to protons
steps.narration: Atomic number defines the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.

steps.title: State proton count
steps.narration: Therefore the isotope has fifteen protons.

teach.title: List given numbers
teach.narration: Write down the atomic number fifteen and mass number thirty-one. Notice that the mass number is extra information we do not need just to count protons.

teach.title: Recall atomic number
teach.narration: By definition, the atomic number tells us how many protons sit inside the nucleus, because protons identify the element.

teach.title: Check mass number
teach.narration: The mass number thirty-one is the sum of protons and neutrons. You would only use it if asked for neutrons, by subtracting fifteen from thirty-one.

teach.title: Read proton count
teach.narration: Since the atomic number is fifteen, the nucleus contains fifteen protons.

steps.title: Dissociate the salt
steps.narration: In water, the double salt splits into potassium, aluminium, and sulfate ions.

steps.title: Pick positive ions
steps.narration: Cations are positively charged ions, which are potassium and aluminium.

steps.title: Count cation species
steps.narration: That gives two different cation species.

teach.title: Inspect the formula
teach.narration: Look at the metals and polyatomic groups in the double salt. It contains potassium, aluminium, and sulfate groups.

teach.title: Write dissociation
teach.narration: When dissolved in water, the ionic crystal separates into free aqueous ions while keeping each sulfate group intact.

teach.title: Separate cations and anions
teach.narration: Cations are positively charged ions, whereas sulfate is negatively charged, so sulfate is an anion and must not be counted.

teach.title: Count the species
teach.narration: Potassium ion and aluminium ion are two distinct types of positive ions, so two different cation species are present.

steps.title: Draw straight chain
steps.narration: Join all four carbons in one straight chain to make butane.

steps.title: Draw branched chain
steps.narration: Put three carbons in a chain with one methyl branch on the middle carbon.

steps.title: Count distinct isomers
steps.narration: No other carbon skeleton is possible, so there are two structural isomers.

teach.title: Identify the formula
teach.narration: Check the hydrogen count: four carbons with ten hydrogens fits the saturated alkane pattern, so only single bonds exist.

teach.title: Build four-carbon chain
teach.narration: First arrange all four carbons in one continuous line. That gives our first isomer, normal butane.

teach.title: Shorten and branch
teach.narration: Shorten the main chain to three carbons and attach the fourth carbon to the middle carbon. Putting it on an end carbon just bends the straight chain without making a new isomer.

teach.title: Count distinct isomers
teach.narration: Since a two-carbon main chain cannot hold two branches without extending to three carbons, only two distinct structural isomers exist.

steps.title: Find dry gas pressure
steps.narration: Subtract five millimetres of mercury for water vapour to get seven hundred and sixty.

steps.title: Convert to kelvin
steps.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to ten and zero to get two hundred and eighty-three kelvin and two hundred and seventy-three kelvin.

steps.title: Apply Charles's law
steps.narration: Because dry pressure equals seven hundred and sixty, multiply fifty by two hundred and seventy-three over two hundred and eighty-three.

steps.title: Calculate dry volume
steps.narration: Evaluate the fraction to get forty-eight point two three cubic centimetres.

teach.title: List initial conditions
teach.narration: Record the measured volume of fifty cubic centimetres and total pressure of seven hundred and sixty-five millimetres of mercury at ten degrees Celsius.

teach.title: Subtract vapour pressure
teach.narration: By Dalton's law, gas collected over water includes water vapour pressure. Subtract five millimetres of mercury so only the dry gas pressure remains.

teach.title: Convert to kelvin
teach.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to each Celsius reading because gas laws require absolute kelvin temperatures.

teach.title: Write combined gas law
teach.narration: Use the combined gas law, and notice that the dry starting pressure and final pressure are both seven hundred and sixty millimetres of mercury, so pressure cancels out.

teach.title: Substitute values
teach.narration: Multiply fifty cubic centimetres by two hundred and seventy-three over two hundred and eighty-three since cooling shrinks the volume.

teach.title: Calculate dry volume
teach.narration: Dividing and multiplying gives forty-eight point two three cubic centimetres for the dry gas.

steps.title: State volume formula
steps.narration: Gas volume at STP equals moles multiplied by molar gas volume.

steps.title: Substitute values
steps.narration: Multiply zero point zero five moles by twenty-two point four cubic decimetres.

steps.title: Calculate gas volume
steps.narration: The volume of carbon dioxide released is one point one two cubic decimetres.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the amount of carbon dioxide, zero point zero five moles, and the molar volume at standard temperature and pressure, twenty-two point four cubic decimetres per mole.

teach.title: State volume relation
teach.narration: Because every mole of any ideal gas occupies twenty-two point four cubic decimetres at STP, multiply the number of moles by that molar volume.

teach.title: Substitute into formula
teach.narration: Put in zero point zero five times twenty-two point four. Think of zero point zero five as one twentieth, which is half divided by ten.

teach.title: Find the volume
teach.narration: Half of twenty-two point four is eleven point two, and dividing by ten gives one point one two cubic decimetres.

steps.title: Find mole amounts
steps.narration: Divide each percentage mass by its relative atomic mass.

steps.title: Find empirical formula
steps.narration: Dividing by three point three three gives the empirical formula CH2O with mass thirty.

steps.title: Scale to molecular formula
steps.narration: Divide one hundred and eighty by thirty to get six, giving C6H12O6.

teach.title: Assume 100 g sample
teach.narration: Treat the percentages as grams in a one-hundred-gram sample so we can convert masses straight into moles.

teach.title: Divide by atomic mass
teach.narration: Divide each element's mass by its atomic mass because chemical formulas count atoms in moles, not grams.

teach.title: Find simplest ratio
teach.narration: Divide all three mole values by the smallest number, three point three three, to turn them into whole-number subscripts.

teach.title: Find empirical mass
teach.narration: Add the atomic masses in CH2O to find the mass of one empirical unit, which is thirty.

teach.title: Compare molecular mass
teach.narration: Divide the given relative molecular mass of one hundred and eighty by thirty to see how many empirical units make one real molecule.

teach.title: Write molecular formula
teach.narration: Multiply each subscript in CH2O by six to obtain the molecular formula, C6H12O6.

steps.title: Find total charge
steps.narration: Multiply five amperes by one hundred and ninety-three seconds to get nine hundred and sixty-five coulombs.

steps.title: Find moles of electrons
steps.narration: Divide by ninety-six thousand five hundred to get zero point zero one mole of electrons.

steps.title: Use 4 electrons per O₂
steps.narration: Four moles of electrons release one mole of oxygen gas, giving zero point zero zero two five mole.

steps.title: Convert to volume
steps.narration: Multiply by twenty-two point four to get zero point zero five six cubic decimetres.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the current of five amperes and time of one hundred and ninety-three seconds. We will convert current and time into charge, then moles of electrons, then oxygen volume.

teach.title: Calculate electric charge
teach.narration: Charge equals current times time because amperes measure coulombs flowing each second. That gives nine hundred and sixty-five coulombs.

teach.title: Find electron moles
teach.narration: Divide by Faraday's constant, ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole, to see how many moles of electrons passed through the water.

teach.title: Write anode equation
teach.narration: At the anode, four hydroxide ions lose four electrons to form one oxygen molecule, so every molecule of oxygen needs four electrons.

teach.title: Find moles of oxygen
teach.narration: Divide the electron moles by four according to the four-to-one ratio in the half-equation.

teach.title: Find volume at STP
teach.narration: Multiply the moles of oxygen by the STP molar volume, twenty-two point four cubic decimetres, to get zero point zero five six cubic decimetres.

steps.title: Find moles of copper
steps.narration: Divide ten point zero grams by sixty-four to get the moles of copper.

steps.title: Check electron ratio
steps.narration: Each copper two plus ion takes two electrons to form copper metal.

steps.title: Multiply by Faraday
steps.narration: Multiply twice the copper moles by ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs.

steps.title: Calculate total charge
steps.narration: Evaluating the product gives thirty thousand one hundred and fifty-six point three coulombs.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the ten point zero grams of copper to deposit, copper's atomic mass of sixty-four, and Faraday's constant.

teach.title: Convert mass to moles
teach.narration: Divide the mass by the molar mass of copper because electric charge depends on the number of atoms deposited, not directly on mass.

teach.title: Write cathode equation
teach.narration: A copper two plus ion carries a plus two charge, so it needs two electrons to become a neutral copper atom.

teach.title: Find electron moles
teach.narration: Double the moles of copper because two moles of electrons are needed for every mole of copper plated.

teach.title: Calculate charge
teach.narration: Multiply zero point three one two five moles of electrons by ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole to get thirty thousand one hundred and fifty-six point three coulombs.

steps.title: Find molecular mass
steps.narration: Double the vapour density of thirty-nine to get a molecular mass of seventy-eight.

steps.title: Find empirical mass
steps.narration: Add twelve and one to get thirteen for one CH empirical unit.

steps.title: Scale to molecular formula
steps.narration: Divide seventy-eight by thirteen to get six, giving C6H6.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the empirical formula CH and the vapour density of thirty-nine relative to hydrogen.

teach.title: Find molecular mass
teach.narration: Relative molecular mass is twice vapour density because a hydrogen molecule contains two atoms and has molar mass two.

teach.title: Find empirical mass
teach.narration: Add carbon at twelve and hydrogen at one to find the mass of one CH empirical unit.

teach.title: Find unit multiplier
teach.narration: Divide the molecular mass seventy-eight by thirteen to find how many CH units make one molecule.

teach.title: Write molecular formula
teach.narration: Multiply both subscripts in CH by six to get the molecular formula, C6H6.

steps.title: Read chloride charge
steps.narration: Chloride is a single ion with charge minus one.

steps.title: Sum oxidation numbers
steps.narration: In perchlorate, chlorine plus four oxygens at minus two equals minus one.

steps.title: Solve for chlorine
steps.narration: Solving gives plus seven, so the oxidation numbers are minus one and plus seven.

teach.title: Write ion formulas
teach.narration: Write the formulas of chloride ion and perchlorate ion so we can inspect their charges and oxygen count.

teach.title: Find chloride state
teach.narration: For a single-atom ion, the oxidation number equals its charge, so chlorine in chloride is minus one.

teach.title: Set up perchlorate sum
teach.narration: In a polyatomic ion, all oxidation numbers add up to the ion charge of minus one, and each oxygen takes minus two.

teach.title: Solve for chlorine
teach.narration: Four oxygens contribute minus eight, so add eight to minus one to get plus seven for chlorine.

teach.title: State both values
teach.narration: In order, the oxidation numbers of chlorine in chloride and perchlorate are minus one and plus seven.

steps.title: Balance equation
steps.narration: One mole of sulfuric acid neutralizes two moles of sodium hydroxide.

steps.title: Apply mole ratio
steps.narration: Use the acid-to-base mole ratio of one to two.

steps.title: Substitute values
steps.narration: Multiply zero point one two five by twenty-five and divide by two times fifteen.

steps.title: Calculate molarity
steps.narration: Three point one two five divided by thirty gives zero point one zero four moles per cubic decimetre.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the acid volume and the base volume and concentration. Both volumes are in cubic centimetres, so their units cancel in a ratio.

teach.title: Balance neutralization
teach.narration: Write the balanced equation first because each tetraoxosulfate six acid molecule supplies two hydrogen ions and needs two sodium hydroxide units.

teach.title: State titration formula
teach.narration: Use the titration relation linking concentration, volume, and the balanced one-to-two mole ratio.

teach.title: Rearrange and substitute
teach.narration: Solve for acid concentration and put in zero point one two five, twenty-five point zero zero, and fifteen point zero zero.

teach.title: Simplify numerator
teach.narration: Multiply zero point one two five by twenty-five to get three point one two five, and two by fifteen to get thirty.

teach.title: Calculate concentration
teach.narration: Divide three point one two five by thirty to get zero point one zero four moles per cubic decimetre.

steps.title: Find moles of Mg
steps.narration: Twenty-four grams of magnesium is one mole of atoms.

steps.title: Find molar mass
steps.narration: One mole of oxygen molecules has a mass of thirty-two grams.

steps.title: Match one mole
steps.narration: Equal moles contain equal particle counts, so thirty-two grams of oxygen matches.

teach.title: Find magnesium moles
teach.narration: Divide twenty-four grams of magnesium by its atomic mass of twenty-four because equal moles contain equal numbers of particles.

teach.title: Link moles to count
teach.narration: We need a sample with one full mole of molecules so its particle count equals one mole of magnesium atoms.

teach.title: Find gas molar masses
teach.narration: Hydrogen, oxygen, and chlorine exist as two-atom molecules, so double each atomic mass to get the molecular molar mass.

teach.title: Check half-mole samples
teach.narration: One gram of hydrogen, sixteen grams of oxygen, and thirty-five point five grams of chlorine each give only half a mole.

teach.title: Confirm one mole
teach.narration: Thirty-two grams of oxygen divided by thirty-two grams per mole equals one mole, so thirty-two grams of oxygen has the same particle count.

steps.title: Convert to kelvin
steps.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to eighteen and zero to get two hundred and ninety-one kelvin and two hundred and seventy-three kelvin.

steps.title: Use combined gas law
steps.narration: Rearrange the combined gas law to solve for the new volume.

steps.title: Substitute values
steps.narration: Put in one hundred and forty-six, the pressures, and the kelvin temperatures.

steps.title: Calculate new volume
steps.narration: Evaluating gives one hundred and thirty-three cubic centimetres.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the starting volume and pressures. Both cooling the gas and raising the pressure will reduce its volume.

teach.title: Convert to kelvin
teach.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to each Celsius temperature because gas law ratios only work on the absolute kelvin scale.

teach.title: State combined gas law
teach.narration: Use the combined gas law because volume, pressure, and temperature all change together for a fixed sample of gas.

teach.title: Substitute into equation
teach.narration: Substitute one hundred and forty-six cubic centimetres, the pressures in atmospheres, and the two kelvin temperatures.

teach.title: Calculate new volume
teach.narration: Compute the product to get one hundred and thirty-three cubic centimetres.

steps.title: Find available oxygen
steps.narration: Twenty percent of one hundred and fifty cubic centimetres of air gives thirty cubic centimetres of oxygen.

steps.title: Balance the equation
steps.narration: Two volumes of carbon monoxide react with one volume of oxygen.

steps.title: Find oxygen needed
steps.narration: Fifty cubic centimetres of carbon monoxide needs twenty-five cubic centimetres of oxygen.

steps.title: Identify excess reactant
steps.narration: Thirty is more than twenty-five, so oxygen is in excess.

teach.title: List given volumes
teach.narration: Write down fifty cubic centimetres of carbon monoxide and one hundred and fifty cubic centimetres of air containing twenty percent oxygen.

teach.title: Find available oxygen
teach.narration: Find the oxygen volume first. The remaining eighty percent of air is mostly unreactive nitrogen, which takes no part in the reaction.

teach.title: Write balanced equation
teach.narration: By Gay-Lussac law, gas volume ratios match the balanced mole coefficients. Notice carbon dioxide is a product, not a starting reactant.

teach.title: Find oxygen required
teach.narration: Divide the carbon monoxide volume by two to see that twenty-five cubic centimetres of oxygen will consume all fifty of carbon monoxide.

teach.title: Compare available vs needed
teach.narration: Subtract twenty-five from thirty to find five cubic centimetres of oxygen left unused.

teach.title: State excess reactant
teach.narration: Because oxygen still has five cubic centimetres remaining after reaction, oxygen is in excess.

steps.title: Write molecular formula
steps.narration: One molecule of ethanoic acid contains two carbons, four hydrogens, and two oxygens.

steps.title: Simplify atom ratio
steps.narration: Divide all subscripts by two to get the simplest whole-number ratio.

steps.title: Identify formula type
steps.narration: CH2O shows the simplest ratio, so it is the empirical formula.

teach.title: Count total atoms
teach.narration: Combine the atoms in ethanoic acid to write its molecular formula, C2H4O2, which shows the true number of atoms per molecule.

teach.title: Divide by common factor
teach.narration: Divide two, four, and two by their greatest common factor of two to reduce the atom counts to the smallest whole numbers.

teach.title: Write simplest formula
teach.narration: This reduced formula, CH2O, shows only the simplest whole-number ratio of elements, not the actual molecular size.

teach.title: Name the formula type
teach.narration: By definition, the formula showing the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound is its empirical formula.

steps.title: Find first ratio
steps.narration: Divide zero point three six by zero point two zero to get one point eight zero.

steps.title: Find second ratio
steps.narration: Divide zero point seven one by zero point four zero to get about one point eight.

steps.title: Identify the law
steps.narration: Equal mass ratios in different samples show the law of constant composition.

teach.title: Check first sample
teach.narration: Start by dividing chlorine mass by metal mass in the first sample to see its fixed proportion.

teach.title: Compute first ratio
teach.narration: Zero point three six divided by zero point two zero equals one point eight zero grams of chlorine per gram of metal.

teach.title: Compute second ratio
teach.narration: In the second sample, zero point seven one divided by zero point four zero is one point seven seven five, which rounds to one point eight.

teach.title: Name the law
teach.narration: Because both samples have the same element mass ratio to two significant figures, they obey the law of constant composition.

steps.title: Find total charge
steps.narration: Multiply ten amperes by four thousand eight hundred and thirty seconds.

steps.title: Find electron moles
steps.narration: Divide by ninety-six thousand five hundred to get about half a mole of electrons.

steps.title: Check silver ratio
steps.narration: One mole of electrons deposits one mole of silver.

steps.title: Calculate silver mass
steps.narration: Multiply one hundred and eight by zero point five zero to get fifty-four point zero grams.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the current, the time in seconds, and silver atomic mass of one hundred and eight.

teach.title: Calculate charge
teach.narration: Multiply current by time because electric charge equals amperes times seconds, giving forty-eight thousand three hundred coulombs.

teach.title: Write cathode equation
teach.narration: A silver one ion has a plus one charge, so each silver atom deposited needs only one electron.

teach.title: Use Faraday formula
teach.narration: Divide charge by ninety-six thousand five hundred to get moles of silver, then multiply by silver molar mass.

teach.title: Estimate the fraction
teach.narration: Forty-eight thousand three hundred is almost exact half of ninety-six thousand five hundred, giving about zero point five zero zero five moles.

teach.title: Find closest mass
teach.narration: Multiplying gives fifty-four point one grams, so the closest answer is fifty-four point zero grams.

steps.title: Check electron ratio
steps.narration: Each copper two plus ion gains two electrons to become copper metal.

steps.title: Find electron moles
steps.narration: One mole of copper requires two moles of electrons.

steps.title: Multiply by Avogadro
steps.narration: Multiply two by Avogadro constant, six point zero two times ten to the twenty-three.

steps.title: Write standard form
steps.narration: Two times six point zero two times ten to the twenty-three rounds to one point two times ten to the twenty-four.

teach.title: Track copper state
teach.narration: In copper two oxide, oxygen is minus two so copper starts at plus two, and ends at zero in metallic copper.

teach.title: Find electrons per copper
teach.narration: Each copper ion gains two electrons. Notice the coefficient three in the full equation means six moles of electrons for three moles of copper, which still simplifies to two per mole of copper.

teach.title: State electron moles
teach.narration: Therefore forming one mole of copper transfers two moles of electrons.

teach.title: Convert to particles
teach.narration: Multiply two moles by Avogadro constant because each mole contains six point zero two times ten to the twenty-three electrons.

teach.title: Write standard form
teach.narration: Move the decimal point one place left and increase the exponent to twenty-four to get one point two times ten to the twenty-four.

steps.title: Convert to kelvin
steps.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to get five hundred and forty-six kelvin.

steps.title: Convert to STP volume
steps.narration: Use the combined gas law to find the volume at one atmosphere and two hundred and seventy-three kelvin.

steps.title: Simplify volume
steps.narration: The gas occupies twenty point zero cubic decimetres at STP.

steps.title: Divide by molar volume
steps.narration: Divide twenty point zero by twenty-two point four to get zero point eight nine mole.

teach.title: List initial state
teach.narration: Write down the starting volume, pressure, and temperature, and recall that STP means zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere.

teach.title: Convert to kelvin
teach.narration: Convert both temperatures to kelvin by adding two hundred and seventy-three because gas law ratios only work on the absolute scale.

teach.title: State combined gas law
teach.narration: Find the gas volume at STP first so we can compare it directly with the STP molar volume.

teach.title: Find STP volume
teach.narration: Two hundred and seventy-three over five hundred and forty-six is half, and half of four times ten gives twenty point zero cubic decimetres.

teach.title: Divide by molar volume
teach.narration: Divide by twenty-two point four cubic decimetres per mole because one mole of any gas occupies twenty-two point four cubic decimetres at STP.

teach.title: Calculate moles
teach.narration: Twenty divided by twenty-two point four gives zero point eight nine mole.

steps.title: State Charles's law
steps.narration: At constant pressure, ideal gas volume is proportional to kelvin temperature.

steps.title: Find zero-volume kelvin
steps.narration: Extrapolating the line to zero volume reaches zero kelvin.

steps.title: Convert to Celsius
steps.narration: Subtract two hundred and seventy-three to get minus two hundred and seventy-three degrees Celsius.

teach.title: State Charles's law
teach.narration: By Charles's law, the volume of a fixed gas at constant pressure rises linearly with its absolute temperature in kelvin.

teach.title: Locate zero volume
teach.narration: Extending that straight graph downward hits zero volume when the kelvin temperature reaches absolute zero, zero kelvin.

teach.title: Recall Celsius conversion
teach.narration: Convert from kelvin back to degrees Celsius by subtracting two hundred and seventy-three.

teach.title: State Celsius value
teach.narration: Zero minus two hundred and seventy-three gives minus two hundred and seventy-three degrees Celsius.

steps.title: Find hydroxide level
steps.narration: Complete dissociation gives a hydroxide concentration of ten to the minus three moles per cubic decimetre.

steps.title: Calculate pOH
steps.narration: Taking the negative base-ten log gives a pOH of three.

steps.title: Link pH and pOH
steps.narration: At twenty-five degrees Celsius, pH plus pOH equals fourteen.

steps.title: Calculate pH
steps.narration: Subtract three from fourteen to get a pH of eleven.

teach.title: Dissociate the base
teach.narration: Sodium hydroxide dissociates completely in water, so every mole of base supplies one mole of hydroxide ions.

teach.title: Write as power of ten
teach.narration: Rewrite zero point zero zero one as ten to the minus three so its logarithm is easy to read.

teach.title: Find pOH first
teach.narration: Compute pOH first because sodium hydroxide provides hydroxide ions rather than hydrogen ions directly.

teach.title: Use water relation
teach.narration: At twenty-five degrees Celsius, the ion product of water keeps pH plus pOH equal to fourteen.

teach.title: Solve for pH
teach.narration: Subtract three from fourteen to get a pH of eleven.

steps.title: Identify shell number
steps.narration: Counting K then L puts the L shell at principal number two.

steps.title: State capacity rule
steps.narration: The maximum electron capacity of shell n is two n squared.

steps.title: Calculate capacity
steps.narration: Two times two squared equals eight electrons.

teach.title: Identify shell number
teach.narration: Electron shells are labelled K, L, M, N outward from the nucleus, so the L shell corresponds to shell number two.

teach.title: State shell formula
teach.narration: Use the two n squared rule because each orbital holds two electrons and shell n contains n squared orbitals.

teach.title: Substitute n = 2
teach.narration: Square two to get four, then multiply by two to get eight.

teach.title: Confirm with subshells
teach.narration: Two electrons in 2s plus six electrons in 2p confirms a maximum capacity of eight electrons.

steps.title: Balance equation
steps.narration: One mole of sulfuric acid reacts with two moles of sodium hydroxide.

steps.title: Apply mole ratio
steps.narration: Use the one-to-two acid-to-base mole ratio.

steps.title: Substitute values
steps.narration: Multiply zero point one by twenty-five, then divide by two times zero point five.

steps.title: Calculate acid volume
steps.narration: Two point five divided by one gives two point five cubic centimetres.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the acid molarity, base molarity, and base volume. Keeping volume in cubic centimetres gives the answer directly in cubic centimetres.

teach.title: Balance neutralization
teach.narration: Balance the reaction first because each tetraoxosulfate six acid molecule supplies two protons and neutralizes two sodium hydroxide units.

teach.title: State titration ratio
teach.narration: Use the titration ratio linking concentration, volume, and the balanced one-to-two mole ratio.

teach.title: Rearrange and substitute
teach.narration: Rearrange for the acid volume and substitute zero point one, twenty-five, and zero point five.

teach.title: Calculate acid volume
teach.narration: The top gives two point five and the bottom gives one, so two point five cubic centimetres of acid is needed.

steps.title: Balance equation
steps.narration: One mole of oxygen gas produces two moles of carbon monoxide gas.

steps.title: Read gas volume ratio
steps.narration: At constant temperature and pressure, gas volumes follow the mole ratio one to two.

steps.title: Calculate CO volume
steps.narration: Doubling ten cubic decimetres gives twenty cubic decimetres of carbon monoxide.

teach.title: Balance the equation
teach.narration: Write the balanced reaction. Solid carbon is in excess, so oxygen limits the reaction and carbon does not enter the gas volume ratio.

teach.title: Apply Gay-Lussac's law
teach.narration: At the same temperature and pressure, equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes, so one volume of oxygen forms two volumes of carbon monoxide.

teach.title: Scale oxygen volume
teach.narration: Multiply the ten cubic decimetres of oxygen by two according to the two-to-one gas ratio.

teach.title: State gas volume
teach.narration: Twenty cubic decimetres of carbon monoxide is formed.

steps.title: Find moles of HCl
steps.narration: Multiply concentration by initial volume to get five point zero moles of acid.

steps.title: Find total volume
steps.narration: Add the ten point zero cubic decimetres of water to two point five to get twelve point five.

steps.title: Calculate new molarity
steps.narration: Divide five point zero moles by twelve point five cubic decimetres to get zero point four.

teach.title: List given values
teach.narration: Write down the starting molarity, acid volume, and added water volume.

teach.title: Find acid moles
teach.narration: Multiply molarity by initial volume to find the moles of acid, because adding pure water does not change the amount of dissolved acid.

teach.title: Add the volumes
teach.narration: Add the original two point five cubic decimetres and the ten point zero cubic decimetres of water; dividing by ten alone is a common mistake.

teach.title: Divide by total volume
teach.narration: Divide the five point zero moles of hydrochloric acid by the total final volume of twelve point five cubic decimetres.

teach.title: Calculate concentration
teach.narration: Five divided by twelve point five gives zero point four moles per cubic decimetre.

steps.title: Find mole amounts
steps.narration: Divide each percentage by its relative atomic mass.

steps.title: Divide by smallest
steps.narration: Divide all three mole amounts by one point six seven to get three to eight to one.

steps.title: Write empirical formula
steps.narration: The empirical formula is C3H8O.

teach.title: Assume 100 g sample
teach.narration: Treat the mass percentages as grams in a one-hundred-gram sample so we can convert masses to moles.

teach.title: Divide by atomic mass
teach.narration: Divide each mass by its atomic mass because chemical formulas count atoms in moles rather than grams.

teach.title: Pick smallest mole value
teach.narration: Oxygen has the smallest mole amount, one point six seven, so divide every element by it to scale to whole numbers.

teach.title: Find whole-number ratio
teach.narration: Dividing gives approximately three carbons, eight hydrogens, and one oxygen.

teach.title: Write empirical formula
teach.narration: Place those whole numbers as subscripts to write the empirical formula, C3H8O.

steps.title: Find hydrate mass
steps.narration: Subtract the empty crucible mass to get four point nine eight grams of hydrate.

steps.title: Find water lost
steps.narration: Subtract the heated mass to find one point four four grams of water lost.

steps.title: Convert to moles
steps.narration: Divide by molar masses two hundred and forty-nine point five and eighteen.

steps.title: Find waters lost
steps.narration: Dividing gives four water molecules lost per formula unit.

teach.title: Subtract crucible mass
teach.narration: Subtract the ten-gram crucible first so we only count the mass of the copper two tetraoxosulfate six hydrate.

teach.title: Find mass lost
teach.narration: Subtract the final mass from the starting mass because heating drives off water vapour, so the mass drop equals water lost.

teach.title: Find hydrate molar mass
teach.narration: Add copper sixty-three point five, sulfur thirty-two, four oxygens sixty-four, and five waters ninety to get two hundred and forty-nine point five.

teach.title: Find hydrate moles
teach.narration: Divide four point nine eight grams by two hundred and forty-nine point five to get zero point zero two zero moles of hydrate.

teach.title: Find water moles
teach.narration: Divide one point four four grams of water by eighteen grams per mole to get zero point zero eight zero moles of water.

teach.title: Find ratio per unit
teach.narration: Divide zero point zero eight zero by zero point zero two zero to see that four water molecules were lost per formula unit.

steps.title: Set up weighted mean
steps.narration: Weight each isotope mass by its percentage abundance.

steps.title: Multiply and add
steps.narration: Ninety times sixteen is one thousand four hundred and forty, plus one hundred and eighty.

steps.title: Divide by 100
steps.narration: One thousand six hundred and twenty divided by one hundred gives sixteen point two.

teach.title: List isotope abundances
teach.narration: Write down the two isotopes and their percentages. Because ninety percent is mass sixteen, the average sits much closer to sixteen than eighteen.

teach.title: Weight by abundance
teach.narration: Multiply each isotope mass by its fractional abundance so more common isotopes carry greater weight in the average.

teach.title: Evaluate each term
teach.narration: Ninety percent of sixteen is fourteen point four, and ten percent of eighteen is one point eight.

teach.title: Add the contributions
teach.narration: Add fourteen point four and one point eight to get a relative atomic mass of sixteen point two.

steps.title: Count total electrons
steps.narration: A neutral phosphorus atom has fifteen electrons.

steps.title: Fill electron shells
steps.narration: Two electrons go in the first shell, eight in the second, and five in the third.

steps.title: Read outer shell
steps.narration: There are five valence electrons in the outermost shell.

teach.title: Match electrons to protons
teach.narration: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the atomic number, so phosphorus has fifteen electrons.

teach.title: Fill shells in order
teach.narration: Fill the inner shells first: two fill the K shell and eight fill the L shell, leaving five electrons for the M shell.

teach.title: Locate outer shell
teach.narration: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell because they take part in chemical bonding.

teach.title: State valence count
teach.narration: With five electrons in the outer M shell, phosphorus has five valence electrons.

steps.title: Find hydrate molar mass
steps.narration: The hydrated sodium carbonate has a molar mass of two hundred and eighty-six grams per mole.

steps.title: Find carbonate moles
steps.narration: Divide two point eight six grams by two hundred and eighty-six to get zero point zero one mole.

steps.title: Match acid moles
steps.narration: One mole of carbonate reacts with one mole of sulfuric acid.

steps.title: Calculate acid volume
steps.narration: Divide zero point zero one by zero point one to get zero point one cubic decimetre, or one hundred cubic centimetres.

teach.title: Find hydrate molar mass
teach.narration: Include the ten water molecules in the molar mass because you weighed the hydrated crystals, giving two hundred and eighty-six grams per mole.

teach.title: Convert mass to moles
teach.narration: Divide two point eight six grams by two hundred and eighty-six to find zero point zero one zero mole of sodium carbonate.

teach.title: Balance equation
teach.narration: Write the balanced reaction: one mole of sodium carbonate neutralizes one mole of tetraoxosulfate six acid, while the crystal water simply mixes with solution.

teach.title: Apply 1:1 ratio
teach.narration: Because the mole ratio is one to one, we need zero point zero one zero mole of sulfuric acid.

teach.title: Divide by concentration
teach.narration: Divide moles by the molarity zero point one mole per cubic decimetre to get zero point one zero cubic decimetre.

teach.title: Convert to cubic cm
teach.narration: Multiply by one thousand to change cubic decimetres into cubic centimetres, giving one hundred cubic centimetres.

steps.title: State Charles's law
steps.narration: At constant pressure, gas volume divided by kelvin temperature stays constant.

steps.title: Rearrange for ratio
steps.narration: Set the final-to-initial temperature ratio equal to nine point seven five over three point two five.

steps.title: Simplify the ratio
steps.narration: Nine point seven five divided by three point two five is three, giving a ratio of three to one.

teach.title: List given volumes
teach.narration: Write down the initial and final volumes at constant pressure.

teach.title: State Charles's law
teach.narration: At constant pressure and fixed gas amount, Charles law tells us volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin.

teach.title: Rearrange for ratio
teach.narration: Rearrange to place final temperature over initial temperature, matching final volume over initial volume.

teach.title: Simplify the ratio
teach.narration: Three point two five goes into nine point seven five exactly three times, so the ratio is three to one.

steps.title: Relate VD to molar mass
steps.narration: Vapour density equals half of molar mass, so the lowest molar mass gives the lowest vapour density.

steps.title: Find first two masses
steps.narration: Both ethanoic acid and propanol have molar masses of sixty.

steps.title: Find remaining masses
steps.narration: Dichloromethane is eighty-five and ethanal is forty-four.

steps.title: Pick lowest density
steps.narration: Ethanal has the smallest molar mass at forty-four, so it has the lowest vapour density.

teach.title: Relate VD to molar mass
teach.narration: Vapour density relative to hydrogen equals half the relative molecular mass, so we only need to find which substance has the smallest molar mass.

teach.title: Find ethanoic acid mass
teach.narration: Ethanoic acid has two carbons, four hydrogens, and two oxygens, summing to sixty grams per mole.

teach.title: Find propanol mass
teach.narration: Propanol has three carbons, eight hydrogens, and one oxygen, also summing to sixty grams per mole.

teach.title: Find dichloromethane mass
teach.narration: Two chlorine atoms add seventy-one, making dichloromethane heaviest at eighty-five grams per mole.

teach.title: Compare and conclude
teach.narration: Ethanal has two carbons, four hydrogens, and one oxygen for a mass of forty-four, so ethanal has the lowest vapour density.
